notes.meaning: Bezalel built the outer altar for animal sacrifices using durable acacia wood. It was square, measuring five cubits wide and three cubits high, with a horn carved at each corner so the whole frame was one solid piece. The entire altar was covered in bronze so it could withstand intense heat.
Workers crafted every tool for the altar out of bronze. These items included pots to carry away ashes, shovels, sprinkling bowls for blood, meat hooks, and pans for holding hot coals.

A bronze mesh grating was placed inside the altar beneath its upper rim, resting halfway down from the top. Four bronze rings were cast and attached to the four corners of this grating to hold the carrying poles.

The carrying poles were made of acacia wood and covered in bronze. They were slid into the side rings so the priests could transport the altar during their travels. The altar itself was made of wooden boards and remained hollow inside so it was light enough to carry.

The large washbasin and its bronze base were made from polished bronze mirrors given by the women who served at the tent entrance. In Bible times, mirrors were made of shiny metal rather than glass. These devoted women gladly parted with their personal treasures to help furnish the place where priests washed before serving God.

The builders set up the outer courtyard that enclosed the sacred tent. Both the south and north sides were one hundred cubits long and walled with curtains of finely twisted linen. Each of these long sides was supported by twenty wooden posts set into bronze bases, with silver hooks and bands holding the curtains in place.

The west and east sides of the courtyard were each fifty cubits wide. The west end was enclosed with linen curtains hanging from ten posts set in ten bronze bases, all fitted with silver hooks and bands. The east end faced the sunrise and formed the front of the courtyard.

Curtains hung along both sides of the eastern entrance, with each side measuring fifteen cubits across. Three posts resting in three bronze bases supported the hangings on the left, and three matching posts and bases supported the hangings on the right.

Fine white linen made up all the courtyard curtains all the way around. The posts rested on solid bronze bases, while the hooks, connecting rods, and the tops of the posts were covered in bright silver.

The gate curtain at the courtyard entrance was twenty cubits wide and five cubits high, beautifully woven with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn on fine linen. It hung from four posts set into four bronze bases, decorated with silver hooks, bands, and tops.
Every tent peg used to pin down the holy tent and its courtyard cords was made of bronze. These sturdy metal stakes kept the curtains firm against wilderness winds.

Moses ordered a full accounting of all the metals used to construct the tabernacle of testimony, which held God's covenant law. Ithamar, a son of Aaron the priest, led the Levites in recording this official inventory.

Bezalel, from the tribe of Judah, led the construction and carried out everything the Lord had commanded. Working alongside him was Oholiab, from the tribe of Dan, an expert craftsman skilled in designing, weaving, and embroidering colorful linens.

The total gold freely presented as a special offering for the sanctuary weighed over twenty-nine talents and seven hundred thirty shekels. This vast treasure, amounting to more than a ton of gold, came from the gifts the Israelites received when leaving Egypt.

The silver collected from the community totaled one hundred talents and one thousand seven hundred seventy-five shekels. Every man twenty years and older paid a half-shekel ransom tax, giving an exact count of 603,550 men in the camp.

The builders melted the one hundred talents of silver to make one hundred heavy foundation bases for the sanctuary walls and the inner curtain, using one talent for each base. The leftover silver was used to craft hooks for the posts, bands to join them, and shiny caps for their tops.

The bronze given as a wave offering weighed seventy talents and two thousand four hundred shekels, which was about two and a half tons of metal. This strong metal was reserved for the outdoor courtyard and heavy-duty fixtures.

Craftsmen used the bronze to make the entrance bases of the holy tent, the altar of burnt offering, its grate, and all the altar utensils. They also cast the bases for the courtyard posts and gate, along with all the metal tent pegs.
